nameStory: The "reticulated" in this moth's name comes from the Latin word for "net," referring to the intricate network of lines and markings across its wings that look like a delicate mesh pattern. This net-like design helps distinguish it from other small brown moths that might otherwise look quite similar.
description: The Reticulated Fruitworm Moth is a small, brownish moth in the leafroller family, with wings that span just 15-17 millimeters across—about the size of your thumbnail. Its wings display a beautiful network of darker lines and markings that create a net-like or reticulated pattern, giving it its common name. Like other tortricid moths, it's part of a large family known for their larvae's habit of rolling up in leaves. Despite being called a "fruitworm" moth, the adults themselves don't harm fruit—this name refers to some related species whose caterpillars can be agricultural pests.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive net-like pattern of dark lines crisscrossing the brownish wings, creating a reticulated or mesh-like appearance that catches light differently than plain brown wings

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small wingspan of 15-17mm—smaller than a quarter and easily overlooked unless you're looking carefully

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Forewings are somewhat triangular when at rest, with the typical tortricid moth bell-shaped silhouette when wings are folded over the body

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with the somewhat erratic, fluttering motion typical of small moths, often attracted to lights on warm summer evenings

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a tent-like position over its body, making it look like a tiny brown triangle against tree bark or leaves

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly where their host plants grow abundantly. Look for them in areas with maples, oaks, cherry trees, blueberry bushes, and other hardwoods, as well as in orchards, parks, and suburban areas with fruit trees. They're equally at home in lowland areas and moderate elevations, anywhere their diverse range of host plants can be found.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not typically active yet, though some may emerge in late spring. This is when eggs laid the previous year begin hatching into tiny caterpillars.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time from June through August, when adults are most commonly seen attracted to lights at night or spotted during the day resting on tree bark and leaves.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down, and the next generation of larvae prepare for winter. Look for small leaf rolls where caterpillars may be developing.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity. The species overwinters in the larval or pupal stage, hidden away in protected spots until the following summer.

funFact: Despite being called a "fruitworm" moth, the caterpillars of this species are actually quite the gourmets—they've been recorded feeding on an incredibly diverse menu including everything from apple and cherry trees to asters and blueberry bushes, making them one of the most adaptable eaters in the moth world.
confusionNotes: This small brown moth can easily be confused with dozens of other tortricid moths, but the key is in the name—look for that distinctive net-like pattern of lines across the wings. Most other small brown moths have spots, bands, or solid colors, but few have this intricate mesh-like reticulation.
contextualKnowledge: The name "fruitworm moth" can be misleading since this particular species isn't a major agricultural pest like some of its relatives. The common name reflects the broader group's reputation rather than this specific moth's behavior, so don't worry about them damaging your garden fruit trees significantly.
compareHints: While this is the only Cenopis species commonly found in New England, it can be distinguished from other tortricid moths by its specific reticulated wing pattern. Most other leafroller moths in the region have banded, spotted, or mottled patterns rather than the distinctive net-like markings. The combination of small size, brownish coloration, and mesh-like wing pattern makes it unique among New England's tortricids.
